analysis.one_liner: Funds housing and services for homeless people by taxing luxury home sales, anonymous property transfers, and large corporate landlords.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 16, 2025 with 30 Democratic cosponsors and referred to five House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the session so far.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would authorize roughly $27 billion a year in grants to state and local governments and nonprofits to house homeless people — permanent supportive housing, converted shelters and motels, public bathrooms, library services for homeless people, and mobile crisis teams that respond instead of police. It would condition most of that money on localities stopping the enforcement of laws that punish people for sleeping outside, and it would fund a federal study and grants to help homeless and housing-unstable people vote. The money would come from three new federal taxes: 5% on sales of property worth $10 million or more, 10% on property transfers through entities whose owners are hidden from public records, and 1% on rents collected by landlords with more than about 1,000 to 2,000 units.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are homeless or housing-unstable — including people in shelters, cars, doubling up with family, or paying unaffordable rent — along with the local governments and nonprofits that serve them. The bill defines coverage broadly, reaching people at risk of losing housing, survivors of domestic violence, people leaving jails or foster care, and households spending a large share of income on rent.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes about $27 billion a year for ten years across the emergency solutions grant, continuum of care, CDBG Plus, and FEMA emergency food and shelter programs — a large scale-up of federal homelessness funding, with a priority on Housing First permanent supportive housing.

The new CDBG Plus program may fund construction of housing permanently affordable to people earning 30% or less of area median income, conversion of hotels and motels into housing, public bathrooms and water fountains, and legal and housing-search services.

Conditions most funding on localities no longer enforcing laws that criminally punish people for sleeping outside, and funds pre-arrest diversion programs and mobile crisis teams as alternatives to a police response.

Requires every grant recipient to have a written non-discrimination policy that explicitly covers gender identity, and creates an advisory board for the federal homelessness council on which at least half the members must be people who have experienced homelessness themselves.

Directs the Election Assistance Commission to study what stops homeless and housing-unstable people from voting — including voter ID and address requirements — and authorizes $5 million a year in grants to nonprofits and local governments to help them vote.

The 1% tax on mass landlords does not apply to any unit covered by a rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protection law, giving large landlords a reason to accept those tenant protections rather than fight them.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers and sellers of properties that sell for $10 million or more (splitting a 5% tax), entities that transfer real estate while hiding their beneficial owners from public records (10%), and corporate landlords with more than about 1,000-2,000 units (1% of rent). If the landlord tax cannot be absorbed, part of it could show up in rents.
analysis.who_pays_short: Luxury property owners and large corporate landlords

drawbacks.text: The 1% tax is levied on the rent itself and applies only to landlords with more than 1,000 units in a metro area, 2,000 units total, or 500 units across three or more states; to the extent these costs are passed on, tenants of large corporate landlords would pay part of it, though units covered by rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income laws are exempt.

The $10 million threshold for the 5% transfer tax reaches well beyond luxury homes — many apartment buildings and commercial properties sell above that price — raising the cost of large real estate transactions generally.

The dedicated taxes feed only part of the authorized spending: the CDBG Plus, emergency solutions, and continuum of care accounts are each authorized at a fixed amount minus whatever Title VI raises, so the full $27 billion-a-year scale depends on Congress actually appropriating the difference each year.

Funding comes with conditions some communities would find intrusive: governments must stop enforcing sleeping bans, adopt formal plans on bias, ID documents, voting access, and property handling, and meet a non-discrimination standard covering gender identity, or they are not eligible for assistance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted: a multi-fold increase in federal homelessness funding aimed at permanent housing rather than police response, paid for by taxes that fall almost entirely on very expensive property, hidden ownership, and the largest corporate landlords. The real risks are practical — the biggest line items are only partly covered by the dedicated taxes and would need yearly appropriations; the landlord tax could partially pass through to tenants; and the conditions attached to funding would rule out some cities that currently rely on enforcement-based responses. Even weighed against those risks, the bill's design directs its costs toward concentrated wealth and its benefits toward the poorest households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill has sat with the five House committees it was referred to since July 2025, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on July 16, 2025 with 24 original cosponsors listed at introduction.
The same day, it was referred to five committees — Financial Services, House Administration, Judiciary, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means — with Financial Services as the lead committee.
Thirty House Democrats are listed as cosponsors, and no Republicans appear on the bill.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the initial referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody has moved: no new taxes have been imposed and no new programs funded. The practical beneficiaries of inaction are large landlords and owners of very high-value properties, who continue to pay no federal tax aimed at housing speculation, while homeless services continue at existing funding levels.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no new taxes or programs

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all 30 cosponsors are House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor — and Republicans hold the House majority, 223 seats to 217 for Democrats.

industries.note: A 1% federal tax on all rent they collect, hitting landlords with 1,000+ units in one metro, 2,000+ units total, or 500+ units across three states. The tax disappears for units covered by rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income laws, so the bill uses the tax to push the biggest landlords toward accepting tenant protections — their gain would come at tenants' expense if passed through.

industries.industry: Luxury and large-scale real estate owners
industries.note: A 5% excise tax on any sale or exchange of property realizing $10 million or more, split between buyer and seller. The threshold reaches beyond mansions into large apartment and commercial buildings, and the revenue funds the bill's housing programs.

industries.industry: Anonymous property-owning entities (shell companies and trusts)
industries.note: A 10% tax on real estate transfers to or from any entity whose beneficial owners are not available in freely accessible public records — unless the entity registers in the legal entity identifier program. This targets hidden ownership of property directly, with the revenue again funding housing.

industries.industry: Homeless services nonprofits and affordable housing providers
industries.note: They would administer most of the new grant funding — emergency shelter, continuum of care, CDBG Plus construction, library pilot programs, and legal services — and gain a permanently authorized federal interagency council with a board that includes people who have experienced homelessness.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority, no Republican cosponsor, and the bill parked across five committees since July 2025 with no committee action, it is very unlikely to get a hearing or floor vote in this Congress; comprehensive bills with purely one-party progressive support rarely advance past referral.
